title: The Rich Fool and Other Warnings
hook: Does 'this night your soul is required of you' describe a soul dragged to hell?
tldr: The rich fool dies suddenly and loses everything he hoarded; the parable says nothing about where he goes next. Its target is greed. The millstone and 'salted with fire' sayings in Mark 9 are aimed at disciples arguing about greatness and harming 'little ones.' They warn about how we treat others now.
big_idea: These warnings target greed and pride now, not a map of the afterlife.

points.title: It starts with a family feud
points.text: A man asks Jesus to make his brother split an inheritance. Jesus refuses to arbitrate and warns against every kind of greed: life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.

points.title: A man talking only to himself
points.text: The farmer's bumper crop leads to bigger barns and a speech to his own soul: relax, eat, drink, be merry. Commentators note he consults no one and mentions no one but himself.

points.title: Required means death, not hell
points.text: 'This night your soul is required' means his life ends tonight; the NLT simply says 'You will die this very night.' The question that follows is who gets his stuff, not where he goes.

points.title: An old wisdom lesson
points.text: Psalm 49, Ecclesiastes and Sirach 11:18-19 all teach that wealth cannot ransom a life and that the hoarder does not know when he will die. Jesus retells a familiar Jewish wisdom theme.

points.title: The millstone protects little ones
points.text: Jesus says it would be better to be drowned with a donkey-turned millstone than to make a 'little one' who believes stumble. It is hyperbole about how serious harming the vulnerable is.

points.title: Salted with fire
points.text: Every sacrifice was salted (Leviticus 2:13). Calvin noted salt and fire both purify. Most read Mark 9:49 as refining trials for disciples, ending in 'be at peace with one another.'

sections.h: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance
sections.summary: Someone in the crowd asks Jesus to rule in an inheritance dispute, a matter governed by laws like Numbers 27 and Deuteronomy 21. Jesus asks who made him judge between them. Then he warns the crowd to guard against every kind of greed, because life is not measured by possessions.

sections.h: The parable of the rich fool
sections.summary: A rich man's land yields a huge harvest. He reasons with himself: tear down the barns, build bigger ones, store everything, then say to his soul, you have plenty for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. Working Preacher notes he talks only to himself and refers only to himself. He is not condemned for farming or saving but for living only for himself.

God calls him a fool: this very night his soul (psychē, life) is demanded from him. The Greek verb is plural, 'they demand'; some take it as impersonal, others supply angels. Translations range from 'your soul is required' to 'you will die this very night.' The follow-up question is who will own what he stored up.

Jesus concludes: so is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. He goes on to tell disciples not to worry, to sell possessions and give to the poor, and to store treasure in heaven that no thief takes. The cure for the fool's error is generosity, not fear of torment.

Psalm 49 says wise and foolish alike die and leave wealth to others. Ecclesiastes laments leaving one's labor to someone else and speaks of eating, drinking and being glad. Sirach 11:18-19 describes a man who grows rich by stinginess and plans to enjoy it, not knowing when he will die. A shorter version appears in the Gospel of Thomas, saying 63.

Luke 12:20 never mentions hell. Some preachers say the farmer went to hell forever, but they support it with Hebrews 9:27 or by borrowing the rich man of Luke 16. Others admit that sending him to hell is not what happens in this story. The hell reading is imported from outside the parable.

sections.h: Who is the greatest? The setting of Mark 9
sections.summary: On the road to Capernaum the disciples argued about who was greatest. Jesus answers that the first must be last and servant of all, and he sets a child among them. John Mark Hicks notes the section opens with this dispute and closes with 'be at peace with one another.' The warnings that follow are addressed to these quarrelling disciples.

Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe to stumble would be better off with a great millstone around his neck, thrown into the sea. The Greek mylos onikos is a millstone turned by a donkey, far heavier than a hand mill. Gill links it to drowning criminals with weights. Matthew 18:6 says drowned in the depths of the sea.

Jesus says cut off a hand, foot or eye that makes you stumble; better to enter life maimed than be thrown into Gehenna, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. That last line quotes Isaiah 66:24, which describes corpses of rebels outside Jerusalem. Readers disagree whether it pictures endless torment or total destruction.

sections.h: Salted with fire, salt in yourselves
sections.summary: 'Everyone will be salted with fire' has puzzled readers; Bratcher and Nida counted at least 15 explanations. It alludes to Leviticus 2:13, where every offering was salted. Calvin, Barnes and Lane see purifying trials for disciples. Gill and Constable say salt preserves the damned in torment. Jesus ends: have salt in yourselves and be at peace.

parable.audience: A crowd including a man in an inheritance dispute (Luke); disciples arguing about greatness (Mark).
parable.setting: In Luke, Jesus is teaching thousands on the road to Jerusalem, warning against hypocrisy and anxiety. In Mark, he is in a house in Capernaum after the disciples quarrelled over rank and tried to stop an outsider.

decoder.traditional: Worldliness that proves a person is unsaved and hell-bound.
decoder.original: Hoarding a windfall for oneself instead of sharing it, in a world where the poor depended on such surplus.

decoder.traditional: The soul is seized for judgment and hell.
decoder.original: Psychē means life. He dies tonight; the NLT says 'You will die this very night.'

decoder.traditional: A hint of the loss of everything in hell.
decoder.original: The Ecclesiastes and Psalm 49 lesson: you cannot take wealth with you; others inherit it.

decoder.traditional: A punishment worse than death awaits: eternal hell.
decoder.original: A donkey-turned millstone, drowning as a vivid hyperbole for how serious it is to harm vulnerable believers.

decoder.traditional: Fire that preserves the damned so they burn forever.
decoder.original: Like salt on every sacrifice, purifying trials that refine disciples into peacemakers.
Humble believers, including the child Jesus set before the status-seeking disciples and the outsider they tried to stop.

visuals.title: What the verse actually says
visuals.text: But God said to him, 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?'

notes.note: A wisdom-literature verdict: the fool lives as though God and death do not matter (Psalm 14:1, Psalm 49).

notes.phrase: This very night your life will be required of you
notes.note: Psychē here is his life. The Greek says 'they demand'; the point is sudden death.

notes.phrase: who will own what you have accumulated?
notes.note: The question is about his goods going to others, not about his soul's destination.

Hebrews 9:27 shows he faced judgment and damnation

Salted with fire preserves the damned forever

items: The farmer dies suddenly and loses his hoard
The parable answers a greedy inheritance request
Millstone is hyperbole about harming little ones
Salt and fire purify, as on every sacrifice

mythfact.myth: The rich fool parable shows a greedy man's soul going to hell.
mythfact.fact: The parable ends with his death and the question of who gets his goods. Preachers who add hell borrow it from Hebrews 9:27 or Luke 16.

mythfact.myth: 'Salted with fire' proves the damned are preserved to burn forever.
mythfact.fact: That is one reading among at least 15. Calvin, Barnes and Lane see purifying trials for disciples, matching Leviticus 2:13's salted sacrifices and the call to peace in verse 50.

mythfact.myth: The millstone saying describes what God will do to offenders.
mythfact.fact: It compares: it would be better to be drowned than to harm a little one. It is hyperbole stressing the seriousness of the sin, spoken to rivalrous disciples.

terms.meaning: Greek word in Luke 12:19-20 translated soul or life; the farmer addresses his psychē and then his psychē is demanded.
A millstone turned by a donkey; a large upper millstone, far heavier than a household hand mill.
To cause to stumble or fall away, rendered 'offend' in the KJV; the sin the millstone warning targets.
Salt required on every grain offering (Leviticus 2:13); some read 'have salt in yourselves' as covenant peace.

quotes.text: But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea.
For everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted with salt.

The farmer's bigger barns and self-talk.

The point: not rich toward God.
The cure: give to the poor, treasure in heaven.
Wise and foolish both die and leave wealth to others.

quiz.q: What prompted the parable of the rich fool?
options: A request to split an inheritance
quiz.why: A man wanted Jesus to make his brother share the inheritance, and Jesus warned against greed.

quiz.q: What does the NLT say in place of 'your soul is required'?
options: You will go to hell tonight
You will die this very night
quiz.why: Psychē often means life. The verse describes sudden death, then asks who will get his possessions.

quiz.q: What Old Testament practice lies behind 'salted with fire'?
quiz.why: Leviticus 2:13 required salt on every offering. Many see purifying trials that make disciples a fitting offering.

objections.claim: The rich fool died unprepared to meet God; Hebrews 9:27 says judgment follows death, so the parable implies he went to hell.
objections.strongest: Jesus calls him a fool and says his soul is demanded, language of a summons. Since the man was not rich toward God, Scripture elsewhere says he faces judgment. Preachers reasonably conclude this foolish farmer went to hell forever.
objections.response: The conclusion depends on texts outside the parable. Luke 12:20 asks only who will own his goods, echoing Psalm 49 and Ecclesiastes on the futility of hoarding. Even a sermon that raises hell admits sending him to hell is not what happens here, unlike Luke 16. Judgment after death may be real, but the parable does not describe its nature, and nothing in it suggests endless conscious torment.

objections.claim: 'Salted with fire' means the fire of hell preserves the wicked, as salt preserves meat, so they suffer forever.
objections.strongest: Verse 49 follows directly on 'their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.' Gill and Constable read it as God preserving the damned in torment. Salt's best-known function is preservation, and the connective 'for' ties it to Gehenna.
objections.response: The verse says 'everyone' will be salted with fire, not only the wicked, and adds that every sacrifice is salted, alluding to Leviticus 2:13. Calvin noted salt and fire share the quality of purifying; Barnes said the passage has no reference to future punishment; Lane links it to faithful disciples in a hostile world. Verse 50 makes salt a good thing disciples should have. Rethinking Hell calls the preservation reading entirely speculative.

objections.claim: If drowning with a millstone is the 'better' option, the alternative must be something far worse than death: eternal torment.
objections.strongest: Jesus contrasts physical death by drowning with a worse fate. Only a punishment beyond death, such as unending suffering in Gehenna described in the next verses, makes the comparison meaningful.
objections.response: The saying is a vivid hyperbole, like cutting off a hand or plucking out an eye in the same passage, which no one takes literally. 'Better than' stresses seriousness; it does not specify what the worse outcome is. In context the next verses point to Gehenna, which echoes Isaiah 66:24's corpses. Annihilationists read that as final destruction, which is indeed worse than drowning; restorationists stress purifying fire. Neither requires endless torment.
